title: Peer Pressure in Early Adolescence: Smoking and Material Comparison
summary: Refusing an offer of smoking from a friend is a skill that needs practice, not just advice. Practice with your son ready-made phrases: a friendly refusal without judging the friend ("No, thanks"), changing the subject, suggesting an alternative activity, or calmly repeating the refusal if pressed. The important thing is to reject the action, not to label the friend as a "bad person," as this preserves the friendship and strengthens his stance, according to HealthyChildren.org. Peer pressure toward smoking peaks in adolescence because the teenage brain changes to focus more on acceptance by friends, reducing the weight of thinking about consequences in the face of his desire to belong. Knowing the harms alone is not enough to prevent it; practice together a friendly refusal without labeling the friend as a "bad person," and keep the dialogue ongoing rather than a one-time warning, according to NIMH. Comparing himself to his friends in terms of money and appearance is not excessive materialism; it is because his brain now focuses more on his status among peers, making the comparison feel heavier. Do not dismiss his feelings with a phrase like "money isn’t everything"; discuss with him the qualities and skills that distinguish him, which are not measured by appearance or spending money.
try_this: This week: Practice one role-play scenario with your son (a friend offering him a cigarette or comparing his spending), and ask him to try his response out loud in front of you before he actually faces the situation.
reflection_prompts: Do you have a ready-made phrase you teach your son to refuse without losing his friendship?
Do you discuss with your son the qualities that distinguish him, or do you just downplay his material comparisons?
